nodes.question: What does the acronym CCS stand for in the context of currencies?
nodes.answer: CCS stands for complementary currency system, which is used to describe a specific unit or system of account that complements the official currency.
nodes.paragraph: Thus, as J r me Blanc notes, we may come across the term "complemen- tary currencies" which reflects the fact that these types of currencies exist alongside national money (or fiat money), whereas their economic and social interests for a community are expressed through the term "community currencies". The emphasis is placed on their social objective by speaking of "social currencies", and some monetary systems can also be Sustainability Science described as "citizen currencies" to underline the fact that they are the result of a formal citizen involvement. Finally, as Blanc notes, the term "alternative" is not new, since several authors were already using it in the mid-2000s to charac- terise several specific economic arrangements (North 2006, 2007; Maurer 2005; Leyshon et al. 2003). Therefore, we use the term alternative currencies because we believe it defines the idea of offering alternatives to national or multinational currency systems, while de facto encompassing the existing specificities. However, in English, the term CCS which stands for complementary currency system is also used to describe a specific unit (or system) of account that complements the official currency and has been developed by a group of agents (individuals, economic and social structures, local authorities or banks) that has formed a local network with a view to accounting for and regulating exchanges of goods and services.

nodes.question: What does the acronym CCs refer to in the context of the paragraph?
nodes.answer: CCs refers to complementary currencies or community currencies.
nodes.paragraph: (Fare and Ahmed 2018, p. 1). As we discuss further in this section, the English acronym CCs is often used as a meta-name to describe complementary currencies or community currencies (Blanc 2011). While it is difficult to account for all of the alternative currencies around the world, primarily because a number of them are not known outside their community or they are not formally studied (Fare 2016), estimations suggest there are approximately 5000 schemes in over 50 countries (Blanc 2018). The vast majority of contemporary alternative cur - rencies began to appear around the world by the end of the 1980s. Moreover, four years after the creation of Bitcoin, there were more than 600 cryptocurrencies in 2013 (Hile- man 2013 ), a number estimated at more than 7500 as of November 20211 reflecting an impressive growth. At the end of the 2000s, in numerous countries the observation of the acceleration of environmental and social crises and the anticipation of the decline of fossil fuels and their cli- matic impacts saw the emergence of the Transition Towns Movement2 with, among other things, the creation of local currencies as primordial tools towards the re-localisation of the economy of communities (North 2013; Stamm 2021).
